title: Tenali Raman Tale 131
summary: A wholesale oil merchant named Chennappa was robbed of two large leather casks containing fifty gallons of pure, expensive pungent black ...
full_text:
A wholesale oil merchant named Chennappa was robbed of two large leather casks containing fifty gallons of pure, expensive pungent black mustard oil from his warehouse.
The next day, Chennappa discovered that a rival merchant named Shankara was suddenly selling large quantities of fresh black mustard oil at half the market price.
Shankara claimed: 'I pressed this oil from my own mustard harvest in my private mill!'

Chennappa appealed to the court.
Shankara produced witnesses who swore they had seen his oil mill turning.
The magistrate was ready to dismiss the case when Tenali Raman stepped forward.

Tenali inspected the disputed oil in Shankara’s shop.
Tenali asked Chennappa:
'Chennappa, what unique traditional method did your family use when pressing your famous mustard oil?'
Chennappa whispered privately to Tenali:
'Master Tenali, my late grandfather always added crushed dried cloves and wild cinnamon bark into the pressing mortar to give our oil its distinctive preservative aroma and golden-amber hue.'

Tenali took a sample of the disputed oil, poured it into a shallow porcelain bowl, and heated it gently over an oil lamp.
As the oil warmed, a subtle, unmistakable, fragrant aroma of toasted cloves and cinnamon rose into the air!

Tenali then took a second bowl containing pure, unadulterated mustard oil pressed that morning in the public market, and heated it.
It smelled purely of raw, acrid mustard, with no trace of cloves or cinnamon!

Tenali turned to Shankara:
'Shankara, you claimed you pressed this oil from ordinary seeds in your private mill.
Why does your oil emit the sweet fragrance of toasted cloves and cinnamon—a secret recipe used exclusively by Chennappa’s family for four generations?
Can common mustard seeds magically sprout cloves in your mill?'

Shankara’s face blanched. He was completely trapped by the aromatic evidence.
He dropped to his knees, confessed the burglary, and led the guards to his cellar where the remaining oil casks were recovered.
King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s sharp sensory observation, which used culinary science to deliver justice.
moral: Nature leaves invisible signatures that chemical reaction reveals with certainty.
